subject: radiology
title: Lung Cavity, Tree in Bud and Ground Glass Opacity

steps.title: A cavity is air inside a mass
steps.tx: **Lung cavity** means a gas filled space inside a consolidation, mass or nodule, created when necrotic centre tissue drains through a bronchus. Wall thickness guides the cause: a wall over 15 mm with an irregular inner edge favours squamous cell carcinoma, while a wall under 4 mm and smooth favours a benign cyst, bulla or resolving infection. The air crescent of a fungal ball sits between these patterns.

steps.tx: A **lung cavity** is a gas filled space inside a consolidation, mass, or nodule, formed when a necrotic centre drains out through a bronchus. Wall thickness points to the cause. A wall thicker than 15 mm with an irregular inner edge favours squamous cell carcinoma. A wall thinner than 4 mm and smooth favours a benign cyst, a bulla, or infection that is resolving. An air crescent around a fungal ball is a separate pattern between those extremes.
steps.say: Necrotic lung tissue that drains through a bronchus leaves a gas filled space inside a mass, nodule, or consolidation. An irregular wall thicker than 15 mm favours squamous carcinoma, while a smooth wall under 4 mm favours a cyst, bulla, or fading infection. A fungal ball with an air crescent sits between those two patterns.

steps.title: Tuberculosis loves the upper lobes
steps.tx: **Post primary tuberculosis** cavitates in the apical and posterior segments of upper lobes and the superior segment of lower lobes, where high oxygen tension suits the bacillus. Multiple thin walled cavities with surrounding tree in bud nodules and fibrosis mark active disease needing isolation and sputum testing. A thick walled single cavity with weight loss in a smoker instead earns a malignancy workup first.

Multiple thin walled cavities with tree in bud nodules mark active disease needing isolation. A thick walled single cavity with weight loss in a smoker earns a malignancy workup first.

steps.title: Air crescent and Monod signs
steps.tx: **Air crescent sign** is the crescent of air capping a fungal ball inside a pre existing cavity, classically an aspergilloma in an old tuberculous space. The ball moves when the patient rolls, which is the Monod sign, separating it from a clot or tumour fixed to the wall. In a neutropenic patient an air crescent instead means recovering invasive aspergillosis as white cells return and dead lung retracts.

steps.tx: The **air crescent sign** is a rim of air over a fungal ball lying in a cavity that already existed, classically an aspergilloma inside an old tuberculous space. When the patient rolls, the ball moves, which is the Monod sign, and that movement separates it from clot or tumour stuck to the wall. In a neutropenic patient the same crescent means something else: invasive aspergillosis that is recovering as white cells return and dead lung pulls away.
steps.say: Air capping a fungal ball inside an old tuberculous cavity is the air crescent of an aspergilloma. The ball shifts when the patient turns, the Monod sign, unlike clot or tumour fixed to the wall. During neutropenia the same crescent instead marks invasive aspergillosis recovering as neutrophils return and necrotic lung retracts.

vis.caption: A mobile soft tissue ball rests in a preexisting cavity, separated from the wall by a crescent of air. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.title: Tree in bud means small airway pus
steps.tx: **Tree in bud** describes centrilobular nodules with branching linear opacities where terminal bronchioles are stuffed with pus, mucus or inflammatory tissue. Endobronchial tuberculosis spread is the examination classic, but bacterial bronchiolitis, aspiration and atypical mycobacteria produce the same bud. The pattern spares the pleural surface by a few millimetres because the smallest lobular branches end before the fissures, separating it from perilymphatic beading.

steps.title: Ground glass still shows vessels
steps.tx: **Ground glass opacity** is increased lung density through which vessels and bronchial walls remain visible, because alveoli are only partly filled or their walls are thickened. When density rises enough to hide vessels the pattern becomes consolidation instead. Ground glass with subpleural sparing and uniform change fits nonspecific interstitial pneumonia, while patchy ground glass with fever fits viral or atypical infection in the right clinical week.

steps.title: Halo and reversed halo signs
steps.tx: **Halo sign** rings a nodule with ground glass, haemorrhage around invasive aspergillosis in a neutropenic host being the urgent cause. Reversed halo, also called the atoll sign, puts ground glass in the centre ringed by consolidation and points toward organising pneumonia. Both signs reverse the usual reading order: the ring tells you the process, the centre tells you the tissue response inside it.

steps.title: Cavity contents checklist
steps.tx: **Intracavitary contents** narrow the cause before cultures return. A dependent mobile ball suggests aspergilloma, an air fluid level suggests lung abscess or infected bulla, and a floating membrane suggests a ruptured hydatid cyst forming the water lily appearance. Rasmussen aneurysm, a pulmonary artery branch ballooning into a tuberculous cavity wall, explains massive haemoptysis and forbids casual biopsy of the cavity wall.

steps.title: Abscess versus empyema split
steps.tx: **Lung abscess** forms an acute angle with the chest wall, keeps a round shape on two views and holds bronchi that end abruptly at its edge. Empyema forms an obtuse angle, looks lentiform and compresses lung with the split pleura sign on contrast CT. The distinction decides treatment: abscess usually answers antibiotics and postural drainage, while empyema needs a pleural drain and often surgical review.
